Romanian attempts to acquire second-hand warships in the aftermath of the First World War

After the conclusion of the First World War, Romania found itself with an extended coastline thanks to the acquisition of Bessarabia, and considerable effort was devoted towards creating a navy commensurate with the role Romania sought to play in the Black Sea and on the Danube.

Allocation of ex-enemy vessels

In July 1920 as part of the allocation of the ex-enemy vessels after the First World War, Romania was allocated six ex-Austro-Hungarian 74T and 82F type torpedo boats, plus one additional torpedo boat which was a replacement for the Romanian vessel Smeul which sank in the Danube estuary on 16 April 1917. The ships acquired were Viforul (ex-74T), Vartejul (ex75T), Vijelia (ex-80T), Sborul (ex-81T), Naluca (ex-82F), Smeul (ex-93F) and Fulgerul (ex-84F). They were handed over to Romania on 19 January 1921 in Venice but didn’t leave for Romania until August-November 1921. During the passage to Romania, Fulgerul ran aground near Cape Kilios in Turkey in February 1922 and was never recovered.

In December 1920, three ex-Austro-Hungarian Danube monitors were allocated to Romania after being interned in Yugoslavia - Ardeal ex-Temes, Basarabia ex-Inn and Bucovina ex-Sava. Ardeal was a 440-ton vessel originally launched in 1904. Basarabia was a 536-ton vessel originally launched in 1915. Bucovina was a 600-ton vessel also originally launched in 1915. All three were armed with two 4.7” howitzers. All three had a long service in the Romanian Navy, being finally withdrawn and scrapped in 1959.

Acquisition of ex-Italian vessels

In 1913, Romania had ordered four large destroyers from the Pattison shipyard in Naples, Italy. After Italy entered the First World War in 1915, all four were requisitioned and served in the Italian Navy. In September 1919 the Romanian Council of Ministers authorised the Ministry of War to begin negotiations with the Italian Navy Ministry to conclude a financial agreement for the re-acquisition of two of the destroyers (Sparviero, ex-Vijelie and Nibbio, ex-Vartezi). The other two were to remain in Italian service on account of war debts arising from arms deliveries. On 1 July 1920, the two vessels were taken over by Romania, and renamed Marasti (ex-Sparviero) and Marasesti (ex-Nibbio).

On 24 August 1920, the Romanian Council of Ministers authorised the Ministry of War to buy six MAS-type motor boats from the Italian Government, together with spare and reserve parts. The unit price for each boat was fixed at 155,000 lire, with 13,000 lire for spare parts for ten vessels. The six vessels acquired belonged to two different sub-types. The first two, M1 and M2 (ex-MAS 268 and MAS 273), were built in the US by Elco. The next four (ex-MAS 348-351) were Italian-built variants of the same class. As they were intended for minesweeping they were not fitted with the 76-mm gun that they had carried in Italian service. Although some were ready for delivery in 1920, this was deferred until Spring 1921 rather than risk towing them to Constanta in Winter. They served until 1929 when they were withdrawn from service due to unsuitability and hull deterioration. Many secondary references list a 7th MAS boat as having been delivered to Romania at this time - MAS 373. It has not been possible to corroborate this claim from Romanian sources.

In November 1920 Captain (later Rear-Admiral) Gavrilescu of the Romanian Navy arrived in Italy as the Romanian Government’s delegate for ship procurement. Among the first vessels the Italian Navy wished to sell was the 7,200-ton cruiser Varese - a member of the successful Giuseppe Garibaldi class. By spring 1921 agreement in principle had been reached. The agreed price was 1,500,000 Italian lire, payable in three equal payments on 1 April, 1 July and 1 October 1922. The fall of the Giolitti government in Italy caused the matter to be delayed until November, and there were further delays over new demands for guarantees covering the second and third instalments. Things appeared to have been fully resolved in January, but on 27 January the Italians advised that the Italian delegation to the Washington Naval Conference had undertaken to observe Article 18 of the Washington Naval Treaty, under which signatory states could no longer sell warships to other navies. The obligations took effect immediately, and the Romanians were advised that the Italian Government could no longer proceed with the transfer of Varese. The Romanians attempted to argue that the sale had already been arranged and financially settled, however the Italians refused. The Romanians subsequently concluded that the new Italian Government had taken advantage of the Washington Conference to make a profit by selling the ship to private industry for more than the low price initially offered to Romania.

Acquisition of ex-French vessels

During the First World War, the United States built 441 110-foot submarine chasers, 100 of which were transferred to France. The French had a naval mission in Romania after the war, and Romania identified a requirement for up to 24 of these vessels. Romania also needed minesweeping vessels to complete the sweeping of mines left over from the First World War. A Romanian proposal that French minesweeping vessels be lent to Romania for at least 6-8 months in return for payment or rent was not agreed. Instead, France offered six ASW gunboats of the Friponne class, but Romania ended up buying only four for financial reasons for a total price of 4 million francs. The vessels were bought under wartime contracts that had not been settled. The purchase was approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 December 1919, and the Romanian flag was raised on 15 January 1920. Originally named A to D, in 1921 they received the names Locotenant Lepri Remus (ex-Chiffonne), Locotenant-Comandor Stihi Eugen (ex-Friponne), Capitan Dumitrescu C (ex-Impatiente), and Sublocotenant Ghigulescu (ex-Mignonne). Once in Romania their mission was to sweep the Russian-laid mines remaining from the war along the Romanian coast. This task was completed on 11 June 1923, and from 1924-1938 they operated as training ships. They survived to see service in World War II.

In 1920, the Ardent class ASW Gunboat Boudeuse was also sold to Romania to provide spare parts for the four Friponne class vessels.

Romania also sought further warships from France - principally to undertake minesweeping operations. Although no further vessels were acquired, vessels offered by France included:

  • The elderly 5,700-ton protected cruiser Jurien de la Graviere
  • The 630-ton Surprise class colonial gunboat Decidee
  • The 360-ton Granit class minesweepers Gres and Marbre
  • The 255-ton Herse class minesweepers Rateau and Coquelicot
  • One or two 342-ton submarines of the O’Byrne type (of the three which had been requisitioned by France while building for Romania during the First World War).

Attempted acquisition of ex-British vessels

In 1919 Britain placed several Royal Navy vessels on its sale list, some of which were quite modern. On 19 November 1919, The Romanian Navy’s Senior Director submitted a memorandum to the Ministry of War expressing interest in procuring second-hand warships from Britain, including one or two monitors and a number of destroyers. On 16 December 1919, the Admiralty sent Romania a comprehensive offer which included the free transfer of the monitor General Craufurd, together with her delivery as far as Malta, and the sale of six to eight M-class destroyers for 10 percent of their original value.

On 13 January 1920 Romania asked the British naval attaché in Romania for more precise information about the ships the Admiralty wished to sell, and the method of payment, and around the same time the British Government offered another monitor, Gorgon, for sale at a price to be determined later, and the British naval attaché suggested that Romania should also ask Britain for an old turbine-powered destroyer to be loaned or sold at scrap value as a destroyer training vessel.

General Craufurd had been built during the First World War to carry a twin 12-inch gun turret that had been removed from the elderly battleship Magnificent. Gorgon had originally been ordered as the coastal battleship Nidaros by Norway in 1912. After the outbreak of war, she was purchased from Norway while still under construction and modified for employment as a monitor.

In March 1920, the British advised that they wanted £400,000 for the ships with their armament. The price covered Gorgon, eight destroyers, two additional flotilla-leaders, and an old cruiser and a destroyer for use as training ships. At the same time, General Craufurd was offered on a free loan for ten years. The Admiralty was willing to offer a reduction if all the ships were accepted, but if that option was taken, Romania would be obliged to purchase General Craufurd after three years for £90,000. The Romanian Naval Directorate concluded that the Admiralty offer was in accordance with the draft naval programme that had been discussed at the meeting of the Council of Ministers and the Superior Army Council on 29 December 1919, and on 7 April 1920, the Council of Ministers authorised the Ministry of War to continue negotiations with the British. Negotiations were to proceed on the following basis:

  • Acceptance of the offer of British ships
  • Payment to be spread over a period of three years, with the first instalments to be paid in raw materials such as grain and oil.
  • A total sum of £490,000 for the ships, plus £110,000 for fitting out, alterations and maintenance until their departure from Britain.
  • Romania would request a favourable offer for a training submarine and some aircraft and seaplanes.

A report submitted to the Superior Army Council on 7 June 1920 proposed accepting the British option of purchasing Gorgon and seven M-class destroyers, one of which was to serve the specialist school for engine-room personnel. This memorandum was approved by the Council of Ministers on 16 June. Gorgon had been recommended over General Craufurd because she was smaller, presented a more difficult target, was faster and more manoeuvrable, and her guns were less worn.

In August the Romanian Government approved the acquisition of Gorgon and seven destroyers for £450,000, payable in three equal instalments in Treasury Bills or in kind, starting on 1 October 1921. An additional £150,000 was provided for work on the Constanta naval base. [note - it has not been possible to work out why the price for these ships seemingly went from £400,000 to £490,000 to £450,000 and then back to £400,000 during the negotiations.]

At the end of August, the British offered to reduce the price of Gorgon and the seven destroyers from £400,000 to £200,000, if payment was made immediately. Romania could not accept any alteration to the payment terms because of Romania’s financial situation, and they requested that their delivery be postponed until spring 1921 when the base would be more advanced and the country’s ability to pay would have improved.

On 22 September 1920, a Romanian commission inspected the ships offered for sale in Plymouth. Their assessment of Gorgon was generally favourable - the ship was modern and suitable for effective coast defence. The same could not be said about the destroyers. Mons required numerous repairs as she had been laid up for a year. Another destroyer, Peregrine, was visited at Chatham and was in a better state of preservation. She also belonged to a newer series of M-type destroyers and incorporated many improvements over the previous generation. The Romanians proposed that at least four of the seven destroyers should be of the Peregrine type. On 20 October, the commission also visited the cruiser Venus, intended as a training ship for the Romanian Navy. It found her well-maintained, spacious, and capable of reaching Constanta under her own power and thereafter fit to make sea passages for training exercises.

Romanian attempts to obtain agreement to payment by instalments in various commodities were rejected. The Treasury representative stated that England’s financial policy is founded on a strict programme of economy, preventing the Admiralty from selling on credit. On 15 December 1920 it was agreed that negotiations would be suspended, to resume when Romania’s economy improved, and Britain asked that Romania negotiate no further ship purchases except from Britain. Following the agreement, Romania proposed to make every effort to acquire Venus first, and the remaining ships in the agreement were to be purchased in subsequent years as resources permitted, but they decided not to accept the request that Romania should refrain from negotiations with other countries while the talks were suspended.

In March 1922 a Foreign Office letter to the Government of Finland terminating negotiations for the sale of second-hand British Destroyers to Finland, referred to the simultaneous termination of negotiations with four other nations as a consequence of the Washington Naval Conference. Handwritten notes on the draft of this letter in the Foreign Office files identify one of those nations as Romania.
